1.pericope_label: Praise ye the Lord. Praise the Lord, O my soul... Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help

schools.summary: Delitzsch places the psalm in the closing group of five Hallelujahs and finds so many points of contact with the alphabetical hymn before it that one author is betrayed, noting also the Greek inscription of Haggai and Zechariah repeated four times, which points to a separate Hallel used in the second Temple. Ellicott works only on the fourth verse, where the Hebrew for thoughts occurs nowhere else and would be rendered etymologically by fabrications, and sets Shakespeare's Antony beside it.

Calvin takes the psalm's subject to be our almost universal disposition to deceive ourselves with expectations drawn from every quarter, and its remedy a hope centred wholly in God; on the address to the poet's own soul he insists the impulse was no volatile fit but a staid affection proved by its effects, applied to his own zeal before he set up as anyone's teacher. Gill hears in the opening the Lord Christ, and in the warning that princes, called benefactors for their bounty, are fickle nonetheless.

Clarke assembles the versional evidence for Haggai and Zechariah, dates the psalm after the captivity and to the moment Cyrus withdrew his order for the walls, and then works closely on two words: that a man's whole existence hangs on the air he breathes, and that 'while I have any being' means his continuance, his progression, his eternal existence. Wesley glosses the fourth verse briefly and plainly.

Henry and Spurgeon both make the psalm turn on who is speaking. Henry observes that David was himself a prince and might have thought praise beneath him, or expected to be adored as the heathen deified their heroes, and answers with the warning of verse 3; Spurgeon pulls himself up mid-exhortation for calling on others while negligent himself, and grieves at the irreverent use the word Hallelujah has lately been put to.

Augustine asks who addresses the soul and to whom, and refuses the flesh as a possible counsellor, since the body is beneath the soul and any soul, however vile, is more excellent than the most excellent body — not in deserts but in nature, as rusted gold is still better than polished lead.

debates.question: Who wrote the psalm, and when?

positions.summary: After the captivity, by Haggai and Zechariah as the Syriac, Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic and Arabic have it — probably at the moment when Cyrus, prejudiced by the enemies of the Jews, withdrew his order for rebuilding the walls, which is what verse 3 answers.

The same Greek ascription is evidence of liturgical grouping rather than authorship: the five closing Hallelujahs formed a separate Hallel referred back to those prophets, and the psalm's coincidences with the alphabetical hymn before it betray one author for both.
There is nothing in the psalm that forbids taking it for David's, whatever the versions and Horsley's title of a thanksgiving of returning captives may suggest.

debates.question: Who is the soul being addressed by, and why does it need addressing?

positions.summary: Not by the flesh, which cannot give the soul good counsel, since any soul however vile outranks the most excellent body in nature if not in deserts.
By a man applying a stimulus to his own zeal before he presumes to lead or teach others, which is how a staid and constant affection differs from a fit of feeling.
By a prince who judged his dignity to oblige him to lead the praise rather than excuse him from it.

outliers.summary: Grieves that the word Hallelujah has been trailed in the mire of late, calling its irreverent use an aggravated instance of taking God's name in vain, and laying the blame on the leaders who countenance it rather than on the ruder sort who use it ignorantly.

Notes that some princes have thought they knew better how to reign by knowing how to dissemble, and that even an honest king's power may be so cramped that he cannot do what is expected of him — as David owned in calling himself weak that day, though anointed king.

themes: Praise ye the Lord. Praise the Lord, O my soul.
While I live will I praise the Lord: I will sing praises unto my God while I have any being.
Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish.

5.pericope_label: Happy is he that hath the God of Jacob for his help, whose hope is in the Lord his God... The Lord shall reign for ever, even thy God, O Zion, unto all generations

schools.summary: Delitzsch and Ellicott independently count the same structure — five lines each opening with the divine name, each of three words, in the terse rhythm prominent in the book of Job — and Delitzsch adds that these lines celebrate the God of the five-divisioned Law with its particular tenderness toward strangers, orphans and widows, quoting Bakius on that Trefoil of God. Ellicott corrects two renderings, reading 'restore' for relieve, with a court of justice possibly in view, and 'bends aside' for turns upside down.

Gill reads the whole catalogue as a description of Christ: the God of Jacob is the Angel who redeemed Jacob from all evil, the eyes opened are those of the men Christ healed and of one born blind, the strangers preserved include the Syrophenician woman and the Samaritan, and the everlasting reign is his — a point on which he notes Jarchi and Kimchi agree.

Clarke keeps the psalm inside the captivity and turns it into consolation: in the son of man there is no saving principle, and this son of Adam returns to the ground he came from, but the God who helped Jacob does not change; Cyrus may alter his mind and God will not; and the same God who has preserved you as strangers for seventy years will bring you out. Wesley gives the two grounds of the faithfulness kept for ever.

Henry counts the fivefold repetition of the divine name as intimating that almighty power is engaged for the oppressed, and answers each mercy in the catalogue with an instance — ravens feeding Elijah, prisoners loosed from Egypt and Babylon, the man born blind, the woman made straight — while also citing Hammond's reading of the whole passage as pointing toward the incarnate Son.

debates.question: Are the blind, the bowed down and the prisoners literal or figurative?

positions.summary: Most probably literal distress and helplessness: blindness is used in scripture both of that and of want of spiritual discernment, but the former suits here.
Historical in the first place — the captives fed, sustained and about to be released — and pastoral in application.
A description of Christ throughout, both of the miracles he worked and of the spiritual sight, liberty and food he gives.
Both at once: the mercies have their Old Testament instances, but the characters are those Christ gave John's disciples, and the beatitude on the man not offended in him answers verse 5.

debates.question: What does it mean that God turns the way of the wicked upside down?

positions.summary: Rather, bends it aside — the word elsewhere is rendered dealt perversely, and the idea is interference: when the wicked man looks along a level road of prosperity, providence bends the course and makes the path crooked.
He subverts or turns them aside: they shall not do all the wickedness they wish, but will be stopped, turned aside, or overturned in their career.

outliers.summary: Notes that the verbs for loosing and opening are transferred from the yoke and from the eyes to the bound and the blind man himself, and that this is the last of the twenty-five beatitudes of the Psalter.

themes: Happy is he that hath the God of Jacob for his help, whose hope is in the Lord his God:
Which made heaven, and earth, the sea, and all that therein is: which keepeth truth for ever:
Which executeth judgment for the oppressed: which giveth food to the hungry. The Lord looseth the prisoners:
The Lord openeth the eyes of the blind: the Lord raiseth them that are bowed down: the Lord loveth the righteous:
The Lord preserveth the strangers; he relieveth the fatherless and widow: but the way of the wicked he turneth upside down.
The Lord shall reign for ever, even thy God, O Zion, unto all generations. Praise ye the Lord.
